title: Superannuation: APRA test trips $7.5b construction fund
full_text:
BUSSQ, the Queensland construction sector superannuation fund with almost $7.5 billion in retirement savings under management, has failed the financial services regulator's annual performance test and must write to its members acknowledging the poor performance of its default product.
It is the first time since 2023 that any superannuation fund has failed the MySuper test, which tracks the investment performance of a given fund's standard option for members.
The MySuper option is the most popular for BUSSQ members; of its 73,000 members, just over 59,000 use that product, and it also accounts for about two-thirds of the fund's total assets.
BUSSQ must notify those members of the failure, in accordance with the rules of the five-year-old assessment.
The assessment has come under increasing scrutiny from the $4.5 trillion pension sector for promoting inefficient, "benchmark-hugging" strategies and skewing capital away from newer, more innovative sectors such as venture capital that take longer to provide solid investment returns.
Should BUSSQ fail the assessment again next year, it would be banned from accepting members into the MySuper product - an outcome likely to lead to a merger with a competitor.
BUSSQ chief executive Damian Wills said he was taking the result seriously, and that the fund had already made significant changes to its investment strategy to improve returns.
"We conducted a holistic review of our investment strategy last year and implemented material changes to our investment strategy and portfolio, removing underperforming investment managers and moving to more indexed equity mandates," said Wills.
The test was introduced by the Morrison government in 2021. It is run by the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority and measures super funds based on their yearly and longer-term returns on investments, after fees, against a benchmark designed to fit its allocation to certain asset classes.
A super product fails if it underperforms that benchmark by 0.5 per cent or more, and the fund must then write to members acknowledging the failure. Last year, none of the 52 default MySuper products failed the test, but seven of 137 trustee-directed products on platforms fell short.
BUSSQ's MySuper failure is the first since retail retirement manager AMG Super flunked in 2023, and the first industry fund failure since 2022.
BUSSQ's fees are also higher than 90 per cent of other MySuper products at $470 a year on an account balance of $50,000. The average cost across the sector is closer to $380 a year.
On Friday, APRA chairman John Lonsdale said the test had "been effective at reducing the number of members in underperforming products".
"This year's results show that pockets of underperformance remain and reinforce the need for trustees to take timely and effective action," he said.
Eleven products offered on big wealth management platforms by MLC owner Insignia Financial, AMP and the Bendigo Superannuation Plan owned by Betashares also failed.
This number was higher than last year, and will reinvigorate calls by those two players to expand the platform test to a wider range of products.
This is because, currently, Insignia and AMP make up about half of those assessed, while products on HUB24 and Netwealth are untested because they are not directly administered by the trustee. APRA noted in its release that its test covered just 5 per cent of the broader platform sector.
A spokeswoman for Insignia said it was disappointed with the results and argued the failure of two options, out of the 33 offered, was because of their higher relative exposure to sharemarkets. "While that approach can deliver strong long-term outcomes, it may not always align perfectly with the benchmarks used in the performance test," she said.
"This outcome highlights some of the limitations of applying the performance test to specialised investment options on wrap platforms."
An AMP spokesman said the test, as it applied to platforms, "is not delivering in the best interests of customers".
"The fact that capital-guaranteed investments, which are achieving their clearly defined risk and return objectives, have not passed [the test] demonstrates the shortcomings," the AMP spokesman said on Friday. "We will continue to advocate for reforms that ensure the test achieves its objectives, including a benchmark which reflects the wider platform market."
Expanding the test to a wider range of products is one option the Albanese government is considering before an overhaul of the test announced by Treasurer Jim Chalmers this year.
Treasury is also considering a new "emerging asset" class to cover venture capital, renewable energy and social or affordable housing projects that take longer to provide a return.
Treasury also has proposed regular reviews of the benchmarks used by APRA, and has raised with the industry an expansion that would include applying the test to retirement-stage products. Such an expansion is widely supported by consumer advocates and the two largest funds, AustralianSuper and Australian Retirement Trust.
